notes.definition: Cloning is producing organisms that are genetically identical to each other or to a parent. Methods include tissue culture and cuttings for plants, and embryo transplants and adult cell cloning for animals.
explanation: Clones are genetically identical organisms. They are produced naturally by asexual reproduction, but humans also use several artificial methods. For plants, the two methods you need to know are tissue culture and cuttings. Tissue culture uses small groups of cells from part of a plant to grow identical new plants. It is important for preserving rare plant species and is used commercially by nurseries to produce large numbers of identical plants quickly. The cells are grown on a sterile growth medium (agar containing nutrients and plant hormones) so that they develop into tiny plants.

Taking cuttings is an older but simple method used by gardeners to produce many identical new plants from a parent plant. A short piece of stem with a few leaves is cut from the parent, often dipped in rooting powder (containing plant hormones), and planted in damp compost. It grows roots and becomes a new plant that is genetically identical to the parent. Cuttings are cheap and quick, but produce fewer plants than tissue culture.

Embryo transplants are used to clone animals such as prize cattle. Cells are split apart from a developing animal embryo before they become specialised. Each group of cells can grow into a complete embryo, so several identical embryos are made. These identical embryos are then transplanted into host mothers (surrogates), which give birth to offspring that are genetically identical to each other. They are not identical to the host mothers, because the embryo was formed by fertilisation of an egg and sperm from the chosen parents.

Adult cell cloning produces an animal that is genetically identical to an adult. The nucleus is removed from an unfertilised egg cell. The nucleus from an adult body cell, such as a skin cell, is inserted into the egg cell. An electric shock stimulates the egg cell to divide to form an embryo. These embryo cells contain the same genetic information as the adult skin cell. When the embryo has developed into a ball of cells, it is inserted into the womb of an adult female to continue its development. Dolly the sheep, born in 1996, was the first mammal cloned from an adult cell.

Cloning has potential benefits in agriculture and medicine. Farmers can produce many animals or plants with desirable characteristics quickly, rare or endangered species can be preserved, and in medicine, cloned animals could be used to produce medicines or perhaps organs for transplants. There are also risks and objections. Clones have very little genetic variation, so a new disease or a change in the environment could affect all of them. Adult cell cloning has a low success rate, and some cloned animals have had health problems or shorter lives. Some people have ethical objections, for example to the possibility of cloning humans, or because many embryos are wasted.
keyFacts: Tissue culture uses small groups of cells from part of a plant to grow identical new plants.
Tissue culture is important for preserving rare plant species and is used commercially in nurseries.
Cuttings are an older, simple method used by gardeners to produce many identical new plants from a parent.
Embryo transplants: cells are split apart from a developing embryo before they become specialised, then the identical embryos are transplanted into host mothers.
Adult cell cloning: the nucleus is removed from an unfertilised egg and replaced with the nucleus from an adult body cell.
An electric shock stimulates the egg cell to divide and form an embryo.
The ball of cells is inserted into the womb of an adult female to continue developing.
Clones have low genetic variation, so they are all vulnerable to the same diseases.

keyTerms.definition: An organism that is genetically identical to another organism.
Using small groups of cells from part of a plant to grow identical new plants on a sterile growth medium.
A small piece of a parent plant, usually a stem with leaves, that is planted to grow into a new, genetically identical plant.
Splitting cells apart from a developing embryo before they become specialised and transplanting the identical embryos into host mothers.
Inserting the nucleus from an adult body cell into an egg cell whose nucleus has been removed, then stimulating it to form an embryo.
A female animal into whose womb an embryo is placed; she is not genetically related to the embryo.
A cell that has not yet differentiated, so it can still develop into any type of cell.

workedExamples.title: Who is the clone identical to?
workedExamples.question: In adult cell cloning, a skin cell nucleus from sheep A is put into an egg cell (nucleus removed) from sheep B. The embryo is placed into the womb of sheep C. Which sheep is the lamb genetically identical to?
steps: The genetic information of a cell is in its nucleus.
The egg's own nucleus from sheep B was removed, so sheep B's genes are not used.
Sheep C only provides the womb for the embryo to develop in.
The nucleus came from sheep A's skin cell.
workedExamples.answer: Sheep A, the donor of the adult body cell nucleus.

workedExamples.title: Calculating a success rate
workedExamples.question: In the experiment that produced Dolly the sheep, 277 eggs were given adult cell nuclei and only 1 lamb was born. Calculate the success rate as a percentage to 2 significant figures.

workedExamples.title: Choosing a cloning method
workedExamples.question: A garden centre wants to produce 10 000 identical orchid plants quickly from one rare parent plant. Should it use cuttings or tissue culture? Explain.
steps: Cuttings need a piece of stem with leaves, so only a few can be taken from one plant.
Tissue culture only needs small groups of cells, so thousands of plants can be grown from one parent.
Tissue culture is used commercially by nurseries for this reason.
workedExamples.answer: Tissue culture, because it can produce very large numbers of identical plants from a small amount of tissue.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think a clone made by adult cell cloning is identical to the female that gave the egg or to the host mother.
misconceptions.right: In fact the clone is genetically identical to the animal that donated the adult body cell nucleus. The egg's nucleus was removed and the host mother only provides the womb.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think embryo transplant offspring are clones of their parents.
misconceptions.right: In fact the original embryo was formed by sexual reproduction, so the offspring are clones of each other, not of either parent or the host mother.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often say embryo cells are split after they have specialised.
misconceptions.right: In fact the cells must be split apart before they become specialised, so each group can still develop into a whole embryo.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think a cloned animal will be the same age as its donor or have the donor's memories and learned behaviour.
misconceptions.right: In fact a clone starts life as an embryo and develops normally. It shares the donor's genes but not its experiences, and environmental variation still occurs.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think an electric shock is used to remove the nucleus.
misconceptions.right: In fact the nucleus is removed from the egg first; the electric shock is used afterwards to stimulate the egg cell (with its new nucleus) to divide.

realWorld: Garden centres and nurseries use tissue culture to produce thousands of identical orchids, bananas and other plants for sale.
Kew Gardens and seed banks use tissue culture to preserve rare and endangered plant species.
Farmers use embryo transplants to produce many calves from a single prize cow and bull.
Dolly the sheep (1996) was the first mammal cloned from an adult body cell, using a cell from the udder of another sheep.
separateOnlyContent: This whole subtopic is in separate Biology only (not Combined Science Trilogy): cloning by tissue culture, cuttings, embryo transplants and adult cell cloning, and the benefits, risks and ethical objections to cloning.
examTips: For adult cell cloning, learn the steps in order: remove the nucleus from an unfertilised egg; insert the nucleus from an adult body cell; electric shock to stimulate division; ball of cells inserted into the womb of an adult female.
Always say whose genes the clone has. In adult cell cloning it is the donor of the body cell nucleus.
For embryo transplants, include 'before the cells become specialised' and 'host mothers'.
Distinguish tissue culture (small groups of cells, many plants, rare species, nurseries) from cuttings (pieces of stem, simple, used by gardeners).
In evaluate questions about cloning give benefits, risks (low variation, low success rate, health problems) and ethical objections, then reach a conclusion.
summary: Tissue culture grows identical plants from small groups of cells; used for rare species and in nurseries.
Cuttings are a simple, older method used by gardeners.
Embryo transplants split an early embryo before cells specialise and place identical embryos in host mothers.
Adult cell cloning puts an adult body cell nucleus into an enucleated egg, then an electric shock makes it divide.
Benefits: copies of useful organisms, preserving species; risks: low variation, low success rate, health problems and ethical objections.

questions.question: What is a clone?
options: An organism produced by sexual reproduction
An organism with a gene from another species
An organism that is genetically identical to another
markScheme: 1 mark: an organism that is genetically identical to another
questions.explanation: Clones have identical genes. Sexual reproduction produces variation, and having a gene from another species describes a genetically engineered organism.

questions.question: Which cloning method is an older, simple method used by gardeners?
markScheme: 1 mark: taking cuttings
questions.explanation: Cuttings need only a piece of the parent plant and some compost. Tissue culture needs sterile laboratory conditions, and the other two methods are used for animals.

questions.question: What is used to stimulate the egg cell to divide in adult cell cloning?
markScheme: 1 mark: an electric shock
questions.explanation: An electric shock stimulates the egg cell, containing the adult nucleus, to divide and form an embryo. No sperm is involved, which is why it is asexual.

questions.question: Which method uses small groups of cells from part of a plant to grow identical new plants?
markScheme: 1 mark: tissue culture
questions.explanation: Tissue culture grows new plants from small groups of cells on a sterile medium. Cuttings use larger pieces of stem; selective breeding is not cloning.

questions.question: In embryo transplants, why must the cells be split apart before they become specialised?
options: Unspecialised cells can still develop into a whole new embryo
So the host mother does not reject them
markScheme: 1 mark: unspecialised cells can still develop into a whole embryo
questions.explanation: Before specialising, each cell can still form every type of cell, so each group grows into a complete embryo. Specialised cells still contain DNA.

questions.question: Calves produced by embryo transplants from one embryo are genetically identical to which animals?
options: Only the mother that provided the egg
markScheme: 1 mark: each other
questions.explanation: The embryo was made by fertilisation, so it has a mix of both parents' genes. The split embryos are clones of each other. Host mothers are not genetically related.

questions.question: Why is tissue culture important for conservation?
options: It increases genetic variation in rare species
It allows rare plant species to be preserved by producing many identical plants
It stops plants from being eaten
markScheme: 1 mark: it allows rare plant species to be preserved
questions.explanation: From a few cells of a rare plant, many new plants can be grown, helping to preserve the species. Clones do not increase variation or form new species.

questions.question: A nucleus from a skin cell of a black-faced sheep is inserted into an enucleated egg from a white-faced sheep. The embryo develops in a third, brown-faced sheep. What colour face will the lamb most likely have?
markScheme: 1 mark: black
questions.explanation: The genes are in the nucleus, which came from the black-faced sheep. The egg's own nucleus was removed, and the host mother only provides the womb.

questions.question: A farmer has a large herd of genetically identical cloned cattle. What is the biggest biological risk?
options: A new disease could affect all of them because they have no genetic variation
The cattle will grow too quickly
The cattle will form a new species
markScheme: 1 mark: a new disease could affect all of them (no genetic variation)
questions.explanation: Clones share the same alleles, so if one is susceptible to a disease, all are. There is no variation for any individual to survive.

questions.question: A farmer splits one cattle embryo into 4 groups of cells and transplants each into a host mother. All develop successfully. How many genetically identical calves are born?
markScheme: 1 mark: 4
questions.explanation: Each group of unspecialised cells develops into one calf, so 4 identical calves are born.

questions.question: A nursery uses tissue culture. Each sample of tissue produces 25 new plants. How many samples are needed to produce 3000 plants?
markScheme: 1 mark: = 120
questions.explanation: Number of samples = 3000 ÷ 25 = 120.

questions.question: A gardener takes 40 cuttings. 34 of them grow roots. Calculate the percentage of cuttings that were successful.
In the experiment that produced Dolly the sheep, 277 eggs received an adult cell nucleus and 1 lamb was born. Calculate the success rate as a percentage. Give your answer to 2 significant figures.
questions.explanation: 1 ÷ 277 = 0.00361; × 100 = 0.361%, which rounds to 0.36%. This very low success rate is one argument against adult cell cloning.

questions.question: A tissue culture lab can divide each plantlet into 5 new plantlets every 4 weeks. Starting from 1 plantlet, how many plantlets could be produced after 12 weeks?
markScheme: 1 mark: 12 ÷ 4 = 3 rounds of division
1 mark: 5³ = 125
questions.explanation: In 12 weeks there are 3 cycles. After each cycle the number is multiplied by 5: 1 → 5 → 25 → 125.

questions.question: Name one method of cloning plants.
markScheme: 1 mark: cuttings or tissue culture
questions.explanation: The two plant cloning methods in the specification are cuttings and tissue culture.

questions.question: In adult cell cloning, what is removed from the unfertilised egg cell?
markScheme: 1 mark: the nucleus
questions.explanation: The egg's nucleus is removed so that the only genetic information comes from the adult body cell nucleus.

questions.question: Give one commercial use of tissue culture.
acceptedAnswers: producing large numbers of plants to sell
markScheme: 1 mark: e.g. used in nurseries/garden centres to produce large numbers of identical plants for sale
questions.explanation: Nurseries use tissue culture to grow many identical, high-quality plants quickly.

questions.question: Describe how embryo transplants are used to produce cloned cattle.
markScheme: 1 mark: cells are split apart from a developing embryo
1 mark: before they become specialised
1 mark: the identical embryos are transplanted into host mothers
questions.explanation: The key ideas are splitting an early embryo, timing (before specialisation) and implanting into host mothers.

questions.question: Give one advantage and one disadvantage of using cuttings rather than tissue culture.
markScheme: 1 mark: advantage, e.g. cheap, simple, no sterile laboratory needed
1 mark: disadvantage, e.g. produces fewer plants from one parent
questions.explanation: Cuttings are easy for gardeners, but tissue culture can produce far more plants from very little tissue.

questions.question: Explain why a lamb produced by adult cell cloning is genetically identical to the sheep that donated the skin cell.
markScheme: 1 mark: the genetic information (DNA) is in the nucleus
1 mark: the only nucleus came from the skin cell (the egg's own nucleus was removed)
questions.explanation: Because the egg's nucleus was removed, the embryo cells contain the same genetic information as the adult skin cell.

questions.question: Give two potential benefits of cloning in agriculture.
acceptedAnswers: many copies of animals with desired characteristics
markScheme: 1 mark each for two benefits, e.g. many animals or plants with desirable characteristics produced quickly; offspring are predictable/uniform; rare breeds or species can be preserved (max 2)
questions.explanation: Cloning copies organisms with known good characteristics, which is quicker and more predictable than sexual reproduction.

questions.question: Explain why adult cell cloning is a form of asexual reproduction.
markScheme: 1 mark: there is no fusion of gametes / no fertilisation (no sperm involved)
1 mark: the offspring has genes from only one parent and is genetically identical to it
questions.explanation: Sexual reproduction involves two gametes fusing. In adult cell cloning, the egg's nucleus is removed and no sperm is used, so only one individual's genes are present.

questions.question: Suggest how adult cell cloning could be used to help save an endangered mammal species, and give one limitation of this approach.
markScheme: 1 mark: take a body cell nucleus from the endangered animal and insert it into an enucleated egg (possibly from a related species)
1 mark: implant the embryo into a host mother (of a related species)
1 mark: limitation, e.g. clones have no genetic variation; low success rate; does not fix habitat loss
questions.explanation: Cloning could increase numbers, but a population of clones lacks the variation needed to survive diseases or environmental change.

questions.question: Two plants grown from cuttings of the same parent are planted in different places. One grows much taller than the other. Explain why.
markScheme: 1 mark: they are genetically identical (clones), so the difference is not genetic
1 mark: so it must be caused by the environment, e.g. different light, water or mineral ions
questions.explanation: Clones have the same genes, so differences between them must come from environmental factors.

questions.question: Describe the process of adult cell cloning in animals.
markScheme: Indicative content: nucleus removed from an unfertilised egg cell; nucleus from an adult body cell (e.g. skin cell) taken; inserted into the egg cell; electric shock stimulates the egg cell to divide; forms an embryo; embryo cells contain the same genetic information as the adult skin cell; when it is a ball of cells it is inserted into the womb of an adult female (host mother); continues to develop; offspring is a clone of the adult that donated the nucleus.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): a clear description in the correct order, including removing the egg nucleus, inserting the adult nucleus, the electric shock and implantation into a womb.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): some correct steps but incomplete or out of order.
questions.explanation: Learn the four steps in order and finish by stating which animal the clone is identical to.

questions.question: Evaluate the use of cloning in agriculture and medicine. Include the potential benefits, the risks and the ethical objections that some people have.
markScheme: Indicative content. Benefits: many plants or animals with desirable characteristics produced quickly; tissue culture preserves rare plant species and supplies nurseries; embryo transplants give many offspring from prize animals; adult cell cloning could save endangered species; in medicine, cloned animals could produce medicines or possibly organs for transplant; cloning research may help understanding of development and diseases. Risks: clones have low genetic variation, so a single disease or environmental change could affect all of them; fewer alleles for future selective breeding; adult cell cloning has a low success rate; cloned animals may have health problems or shorter lives. Ethical objections: worry that it could lead to human cloning; many embryos wasted or destroyed; animal welfare; some feel it is unnatural or 'playing God'. Conclusion: a reasoned judgement.
Level 3 (5 to 6 marks): a detailed and balanced evaluation including benefits, risks and ethical issues in both agriculture and medicine, with a justified conclusion.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): describes some benefits and some risks or objections, with limited balance or no conclusion.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): simple statements of benefits or problems.
questions.explanation: An evaluation needs both sides with reasons and a conclusion. Link the low genetic variation of clones to the risk from disease.
